h1: In-car design where a second of attention is the budget
subtitle: Automotive HMI is one place where an interface decision has a physical safety consequence. We design infotainment and cluster experiences around glance duration and cognitive load, constraints that make most conventional UI thinking actively wrong.

cta.heading: Designing for the road, not the desk
cta.body: Tell us about your programme, hardware and timeline. We'll tell you how we would approach the glance and task model.

sections.heading: Why automotive HMI breaks normal design rules

items.title: Attention is borrowed, not given
items.body: Every glance at a screen is attention taken from the road. Guidance converges on roughly two seconds per glance.

items.title: The user is physically moving
items.body: Vibration, changing light and occupied hands. Targets and contrast that pass on a desk fail on the road.

items.title: Hardware is fixed years ahead
items.body: Screen, processing budget and control layout are locked long before design starts.

items.title: Safety-critical and comfort share a screen
items.body: The hierarchy between what a driver must see and might want is a safety decision expressed as layout.

items.title: Digital instrument clusters
items.body: Speed, range, warnings and ADAS state designed for peripheral legibility.

items.title: Infotainment systems
items.body: Navigation, media, climate and settings structured so common tasks fit a safe glance budget.

items.title: Glance-load analysis
items.body: Task-by-task assessment of glance cost, so distraction is measured during design.

items.title: Day, night and adverse conditions
items.body: Full state design across lighting and glare.

items.title: Multi-modal interaction
items.body: Touch, physical controls, steering-wheel input and voice that behave coherently.

items.title: Design systems for vehicle ranges
items.body: A consistent HMI language across trims and model years.

items.title: Constraints first
items.body: Hardware, regulation, control layout and driving contexts define the design space.

items.title: Task and glance modelling
items.body: Every driver task mapped against the attention it costs.

items.title: Design and simulate
items.body: Interfaces evaluated in driving-simulator conditions, because desk evaluation underestimates glance cost.

items.title: Handover
items.body: Specifications detailed enough for embedded engineering teams.

sections.heading: Selected automotive work
sections.intro: An infotainment interface and a digital instrument cluster, designed within a tier-one supplier's engineering constraints.

faq.q: How do you design for driver distraction?
faq.a: By treating glance duration as the primary design budget. Industry guidance converges on roughly two seconds per glance and a limited total per task, so we model each task's glance cost during design: larger type, fewer simultaneous decisions, information positioned for peripheral pickup, and frequent actions on physical controls where possible.

faq.q: Do you work within existing hardware constraints?
faq.a: Always. In automotive that is the job: screen size, resolution, processing budget and control layout are fixed, and the design has to work within them.

faq.q: How long do automotive engagements take?
faq.a: A single HMI surface typically runs eight to ten weeks. A full cluster plus infotainment programme is a multi-month engagement with validation gates built in.
